title: Not everything is as it seems: neurosarcoidosis presenting as leptomeningitis
case_prompt:
A 39-year-old woman with no prior medical history presented with a 2-week history of gradually worsening frontal headache, intermittent fever, nausea, vomiting, disorientation, and incoherent speech. On examination, her pupils were miotic but reactive to light, with no papilledema. Meningeal signs were positive (Kernig and Brudzinski), and the rest of the neurologic examination was normal. Laboratory studies showed normal complete blood count and liver function tests, but blood chemistry revealed hyponatremia and a low thyroid-stimulating hormone level. Brain MRI with and without gadolinium demonstrated generalized leptomeningeal enhancement—basal predominance and multinodular appearance—with evidence of hydrocephalus. A lumbar puncture yielded straw-colored CSF with polymorphonuclear-predominant leukocytosis, hypoproteinorrachia, and hypoglycorrhachia; Gram stain was negative, and cultures were obtained. 

A ventriculostomy was placed, and the patient received empiric meropenem, vancomycin, acyclovir, and prednisone. CSF cultures remained negative. During hospitalization she developed hypernatremia attributable to diabetes insipidus that did not respond to fluid restriction. She improved neurologically and was discharged on a tapering steroid regimen.

One month later she experienced a recurrence of frontal headache, intermittent fever, nausea, vomiting, disorientation, incoherent speech, polyuria, and polydipsia. Repeat lumbar puncture showed marked hyperproteinorrachia without pleocytosis. Chest radiography revealed a diffuse reticulonodular interstitial pulmonary pattern and mild mediastinal widening.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial meningitis was considered given PMN-predominant CSF pleocytosis and hydrocephalus — “clinical suspicion of SNC infection” — but was excluded because “CSF cultures reported no microbiological development.”
2. Viral meningitis was considered in the empiric use of acyclovir, but lack of viral growth and normalization of CSF cell counts on repeat tap argued against a viral cause — “CSF cultures reported no microbiological development.”
3. Carcinomatous meningitis or lymphoma was considered in a patient with aseptic meningitis and mediastinal widening, but was excluded when supraclavicular lymph node biopsy showed “the presence of noncaseating granulomas, compatible with sarcoidosis.”
4. Neurosarcoidosis was confirmed by histopathology demonstrating characteristic granulomas in lymph node tissue — “compatible with sarcoidosis.”
